articles.title: Your Python Code Returns From a finally Block and Python 3.14 Now Warns About It
articles.excerpt: The save function def save_order(order): It always logged. It always returned. It always said True. Even when the database That is the trap. A return inside finally It throws away No traceback. No err…
articles.body: The save function looked defensive. def save_order(order): try: db.write(order) finally: log.info("save attempted") return True It always logged. It always returned. It always said True. Even when the database was down. That is the trap. A return inside finally does not just return. It throws away whatever exception was on its way out. No traceback. No error. The caller is told everything went fine. The same goes for break and continue inside a finally in a loop. The exception simply disappears. Even a KeyboardInterrupt. Even the error that would have told you the disk was full, or the connection had gone, or the order was never written. This has been legal Python for as long as finally has existed. It is also almost never what anyone meant. Here is what changed.

articles.title: Running a job search with Claude Code and Codex, and what we learned building the MCP server behind it
articles.excerpt: A lot of people now let an AI agent do the boring parts of a job search: finding postings, reading We built ApplyKoala to be that memory: a job application tracker with a Claude Code: claude mcp add -…
articles.body: A lot of people now let an AI agent do the boring parts of a job search: finding postings, reading them, judging fit, filling in forms. Claude Code and Codex are surprisingly good at this. What they are bad at is remembering. Close the session and the agent forgets which jobs it read, which ones it applied to and what it wrote in each form. We built ApplyKoala to be that memory: a job application tracker with a remote MCP server, so the agent keeps the whole search in one place and you can see it on a board. This post is how the setup works and a few things we learned along the way. The setup in five minutes Claude Code: claude mcp add --scope user --transport http applykoala https://applykoala.com/mcp Then type /mcp and sign in.
articles.author: ApplyKoala

articles.title: You Had Two Database Servers Open in Two Terminals and Typed Into the Wrong One
articles.excerpt: Late evening. Replication was broken. You had two terminal windows open. One on the primary. One on the replica. Same prompt. Same font. Same black background. The plan was simple. Wipe the replica's…
articles.body: Late evening. Replication was broken. You had two terminal windows open. One on the primary. One on the replica. Same prompt. Same font. Same black background. The plan was simple. Wipe the replica's data directory and copy it fresh from the primary. You typed the command. Pressed enter. Then noticed the hostname. This is not a hypothetical. On the last day of January 2017, a GitLab engineer did exactly this, deleting data on the primary database instead of the replica, and the company lost about six hours of production data. He stopped it within seconds. Seconds were enough. Here is the mechanism. Designers call it a mode error. The same action means different things depending on a state you are not looking at. The keys are identical. The window is identical.

articles.title: The Bug Reached Forty Thousand Customers and You Felt What You Felt for Four Hundred
articles.excerpt: Two incidents On Monday On Thursday You read both reports. You felt bad About the same amount. The team spent The postmortems One of them Nothing in the room This has a name. Scope insensitivity. In o…
articles.body: Two incidents in the same week. On Monday a checkout bug hit four hundred customers. On Thursday a pricing bug hit forty thousand. You read both reports. You felt bad about both. About the same amount. The team spent roughly the same effort on each fix. The postmortems were the same length. One of them was a hundred times bigger. Nothing in the room said so. This has a name. Scope insensitivity. In one well known study, people were asked how much they would pay to stop migratory birds drowning in oil ponds. Two thousand birds. Twenty thousand. Two hundred thousand. The average answers were about eighty dollars, seventy eight, and eighty eight. A hundred times the birds. Roughly the same money. People were not paying for the birds. They were paying for the picture in their head.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of lightwhile observing Jupiter and its moon volcanic moon Io. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.

articles.title: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says
articles.excerpt: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. Rather, it will go on display as a museum piece, according to company founder and CEO Elon Musk.
articles.body: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas. Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen. "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit .

articles.title: European-Japanese BepiColombo probe arrives in orbit around Mercury today
articles.excerpt: The BepiColombo spacecraft will finally arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.
articles.body: Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. The big moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.
